verses.note: The ruler's reign brings an abundance that reverses the curse on the ground (3:17-19). The prophets use the same picture of overflowing wine for the age of restoration (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18).

The Messiah's peace extends to creation itself. Whether read literally or as a picture of nations at peace (the chapter note sets out both), the passage refuses a salvation that concerns souls alone. Paul speaks of the whole creation waiting to be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:19-21).

The child's hand at the serpent's den quietly reverses the enmity between the serpent and the woman's offspring in Genesis 3:15. The link is thematic rather than verbal, but it fits Isaiah's picture of a world where the curse no longer rules.

Whatever the riddle means, the frame is clear: God will ‘create’ something new, using the verb of Genesis 1. Restoration is presented as an act of creation, not merely repair. Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17 speak the same way, and the New Testament takes up the idea in Paul's ‘new creation’ (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The language of Genesis 1:28 marks restoration as a new beginning. The book's hope is not only return but creation renewed, a theme that climaxes in the Eden picture of verse 35 and in the river of chapter 47.

Eden is the Bible's picture of the world as God meant it, with God and people together. Isaiah 51:3 promises the same for Zion. The hope of a restored Eden runs through Ezekiel's temple river (47:1-12) to Revelation's tree of life (Revelation 22:1-2).

The breaking of the bow joins a line of prophetic promises in which God ends war itself (Isaiah 2:4; Hosea 2:18; Micah 4:3), a peace the New Testament grounds in Christ, who came and proclaimed peace to those far off and those near (Ephesians 2:17).

The promised inheritance is not escape from the world but the earth itself. Read with 19:28 (‘the renewal of all things’) and Romans 4:13, the beatitude points to a renewed creation given to the humble.
Heaven and earth as they now are will pass away. The New Testament hope is not that the world simply continues but that God makes a new heaven and earth (2 Peter 3:13, Revelation 21:1).
The created world has a future in God's purpose, bound to the future of his children. Paul's hope is not for escape from the material world but for its renewal.

Creation's slavery to decay is not its final state. Paul promises that the physical world will share in the freedom of God's glorified children, the Bible's hope of a new heavens and new earth (Isaiah 65:17, Revelation 21:1-5).
